medical.title: Radiology pipeline expanding slower than medicine as a whole
medical.summary: Demand for medical imaging in the U.S. keeps rising, but the number of radiologists available to read those images has barely budged relative to the population, according to a study published in the Journal of the American College of Radiology.

medical.title: Training the mind and emotional skills may support brain health after 65
medical.summary: Education, intellectually stimulating work and an active lifestyle help preserve cognitive abilities in adults over 65 and lead to more effective verbal expression and stronger cognitive performance. But there is another important factor: emotions. The way we recognize and interpret them can significantly influence the efficiency of cognitive processes as we age.

medical.title: Ghanaian adults' diets fall short on sustainability, survey finds
medical.summary: There has been a rapid increase in cardiovascular and metabolic conditions in sub-Saharan Africa. What is the link between sustainable diets that are nutritious, environmentally friendly, economically affordable and socioculturally acceptable, and cardiometabolic conditions? An international research team led by Prof. Dr. Ina Danquah, Hertz Chair for Innovation for Planetary Health in the Transdisciplinary Research Area "Sustainable Futures" and director at the Center for Development Research (ZEF) at the University of Bonn, investigated this question among Ghanaian adults living in various locations for an article published in The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition.

medical.title: Study highlights risk groups for a severe side effect of diabetes treatment
medical.summary: Patients with type 2 diabetes who have high blood glucose levels, low body weight or a history of ketoacidosis are at increased risk of developing this serious condition when treated with so-called SGLT2 inhibitors. A study led by researchers at Karolinska Institutet also shows that the risk persists throughout the entire course of treatment.

medical.title: Cancer cachexia: How a tumor protein drives wasting in the body
medical.summary: Researchers at Helmholtz Munich, the Heidelberg Faculty of Medicine at Heidelberg University, the German Center for Diabetes Research (DZD) and the Technical University of Munich (TUM) have identified a previously unknown mechanism that can drive cancer cachexia—a wasting process in the body that primarily affects muscle and fat tissue.

medical.title: First touch, faster play: Study reveals the body and ball movements associated with quicker soccer passing
medical.summary: In soccer, the quality of the first touch is integral to shaping a player's subsequent actions. Despite its importance, there is limited scientific evidence regarding which specific movement characteristics are associated with effective first-touch performance.

medical.title: How does the cancer drug Keytruda work? And how is it different from chemo?
medical.summary: From today, the Australian government will expand Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) access to the drug Keytruda for three additional types of cancer.

medical.title: Your smartwatch may be lying to you about how many calories you burned
medical.summary: If you're depending on your smartwatch to tell you the truth about how many calories you burned during a workout—well, don't.

medical.title: Peppermint oil lowers blood pressure in just 20 days
medical.summary: Peppermint oil may have an unexpected benefit for people with mildly high blood pressure. Adults who took a small dose twice daily for 20 days saw their systolic blood pressure fall by an average of 8.5 mmHg, while a placebo group showed little change. Researchers say the inexpensive oil could eventually provide a simple additional option for managing elevated blood pressure.

medical.title: Exercise may work better for keeping weight off than losing it
medical.summary: Exercise may not be a powerful weight-loss tool on its own, but it appears to play a much bigger role in preventing lost weight from returning. By preserving muscle, supporting metabolism, improving fat burning, and regulating appetite and blood sugar, regular activity can make long-term weight maintenance easier.

medical.title: Multilingual people may have brains up to 13 years younger
medical.summary: People who speak several languages may have brains that age more slowly, with four-language speakers showing brains that appeared about 13 years younger than those of monolinguals. Starting earlier and becoming highly fluent were also linked to a stronger effect.

medical.title: This yeast supplement may boost cancer-fighting immunity
medical.summary: A simple yeast-based food supplement may help restore the immune system’s ability to fight cancer, according to new research in mice. Scientists found that yeast beta-glucan reprogrammed early immune cells in the bone marrow, leading to stronger, longer-lasting cancer-fighting responses against colorectal, skin, and breast cancer cells.

medical.title: Tooth count may predict survival after pancreatic cancer surgery
medical.summary: Pancreatic cancer patients with at least 21 natural teeth survived nearly two years longer after surgery than those with fewer teeth in a study of 339 people. Researchers suspect tooth loss may reflect decades of inflammation, frailty, nutrition, and other factors tied to the body’s overall resilience.

medical.title: This gut microbe may help keep you strong as you age
medical.summary: Scientists have linked a specific gut bacterium, Roseburia inulinivorans, to stronger muscles in both humans and mice. Older adults who carried it had 29% greater handgrip strength, while treated mice gained about 30% more grip strength and developed larger, more fast-twitch muscle fibers. The bacterium was also less common in older people. Researchers say it could eventually become a probiotic candidate for helping combat age-related muscle loss.

science.title: Single amino acid swap expands nanoparticle vaccine approach to influenza viruses
science.summary: Influenza viruses constantly shapeshift to evade recognition by the immune system. This shapeshifting occurs in critical proteins like hemagglutinin (HA), which controls how the virus attaches to human cells before entering them. Influenza viruses can evade immunity in two major ways: through the gradual accumulation of mutations that make HA harder for the immune system to recognize or through reassortment events that can introduce substantially different viral proteins and potentially lead to flu pandemics. To address this challenge, seasonal flu vaccines remain the primary approach because they can be developed to target the flu viruses circulating most predominantly in a given season.

science.title: Algorithm improves detection of differentially expressed genes in large single-cell trajectory data sets
science.summary: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is a method for measuring gene expression in individual cells, allowing observation of various cellular processes, including cell differentiation, the cell cycle and stimulus response, for each unique cell instead of averaging across millions of cells. It provides high-resolution snapshots of biological processes. However, it does not track the same cell continuously over time. To address this limitation, trajectory inference approaches have been developed that computationally arrange cellular snapshots along an inferred developmental trajectory known as pseudotime.

science.title: Firelight may have sparked human storytelling by extending social hours
science.summary: New research from the University of St Andrews has developed a novel hypothesis of how firelight was critical to the evolution of sophisticated storytelling.

science.title: Muddying the waters makes stickleback fish more coordinated, study finds
science.summary: Stickleback fish can change their social behavior to help them find food in cloudy water, according to a new University of Bristol study published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

science.title: Survey reveals marine biodiversity hotspot needs protection
science.summary: An environmental DNA study by a multi-institutional research collaboration has revealed distinct regions of extraordinary marine biodiversity that can help inform management of a proposed marine park in Western Australia's Exmouth Gulf.

science.title: LEDs let archaeologists see the past in a new light
science.summary: An archaeological excavation is a little like eating a layered cake: Once you have removed a layer, you cannot put it back. The problem becomes even trickier if two layers look almost exactly the same. Researchers from Aarhus University and Moesgaard Museum in Denmark have now developed a relatively inexpensive multispectral imaging system that gives archaeologists more ways of looking at the soil before they dig into it.

science.title: To promote climate action, emotion may matter more than information
science.summary: Every year, public authorities and nongovernmental organizations spend millions on communication campaigns designed to encourage people to take action on climate change. But which strategies work best? Should campaigns rely on fear or positive messages, prioritize facts or appeal to emotions, and focus on words or visuals?

science.title: Giant impact could have formed an intact moon within five hours, simulations suggest
science.summary: New Southwest Research Institute (SwRI) modeling, conducted in collaboration with scientists at the University of Arizona, shows fundamental differences in how the moon may have formed from the giant impact that created the Earth–moon system. The new results used state-of-the-art computational techniques that factor in the material strength of the two colliding planets. These impact simulations could change how researchers understand moon formation and may help constrain the timing of the event. The research is published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

science.title: Elementary school teachers report increased student hunger and anxiety after universal free school meals ended
science.summary: A recent study published in the Journal of Nutrition Education and Behavior explored elementary school teachers' experiences before and after the end of the federal universal free school meals (UFSM) policy. Researchers found that teachers perceived the policy had helped reduce student hunger and family stress, while its expiration was associated with increased hunger, anxiety about meal costs and decreased participation in school meal programs.

science.title: Salt of the Earth: How Egypt's coastal sabkhas tell a story of climate and change
science.summary: Have you ever walked across a salt flat so expansive it feels like another planet? That's what it's like standing in Egypt's coastal sabkhas—those otherworldly landscapes where the ground crunches beneath your feet and the air shimmers with heat. These aren't just barren wastelands; they're living laboratories that record the pulse of our changing climate.

science.title: Canada's Labrador Shelf preserves climate records once thought erased by ice
science.summary: The Labrador Shelf is a shallow marine area on the margin of the Labrador Sea in the North Atlantic off the east coast of Canada. During the last ice age, this region was covered by the Laurentide Ice Sheet, one of the largest ice masses in Earth's history, which once covered vast parts of North America.

science.title: A roadmap for animal-free chemical testing
science.summary: For many years, the European Union has pursued a policy aimed at the replacement, reduction and refinement of animal testing (the 3Rs principle). To put the ethical principle of the 3Rs into practice, the European Commission has published a roadmap for the gradual phaseout of animal testing in the safety assessment of chemicals.

environment.summary: If you sit in an Australian park or garden for long enough, chances are you might catch a flash of brilliant feathers out of the corner of your eye: the superb fairywren. The South African section of the kelp forest stretches around 800 miles or 1,300 kilometers, straddling two coasts and two oceans. environment.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals ancient waterproofing secrets
environment.summary: Scientists analyzing a 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck found that its hull was coated with pine tar and, in one area, a mixture of tar and beeswax. Pollen trapped in those ancient coatings acted like a geographic fingerprint, revealing the landscapes surrounding the ship when repairs were made.

environment.title: A lost mega-cliff may explain the Grand Canyon’s missing billion years
environment.summary: A colossal cliff system created as the supercontinent Rodinia broke apart may have exposed the heart of the Grand Canyon nearly a billion years before the Colorado River carved it. The ancient landscape could also help explain why enormous sections of North America’s geological record appear to be missing.

environment.title: “One-in-a-million” sea creature fossil preserves soft tissue for 450 million years
environment.summary: Scientists have identified exceptionally rare soft tissue preserved in a 450-million-year-old crinoid fossil, more than 200 million years older than the first dinosaurs. Its delicate tube feet offer a remarkable new window into how some of Earth’s earliest reef animals lived, fed, and evolved.

environment.title: A new Ice Age species was hiding in la brea tar pits fossils for decades
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered a new extinct amphibian species hiding in the fossil collections of Los Angeles’ La Brea Tar Pits. Named Spea labreae, the Ice Age spadefoot toad is an exceptionally rare find—only one other extinct Pleistocene amphibian has ever been identified in North America. Its bones had been sitting in collections since the 1950s before a researcher noticed features that set it apart from known species.

mix_items.title: Radiology pipeline expanding slower than medicine as a whole
mix_items.summary: Demand for medical imaging in the U.S. keeps rising, but the number of radiologists available to read those images has barely budged relative to the population, according to a study published in the Journal of the American College of Radiology.

mix_items.title: Single amino acid swap expands nanoparticle vaccine approach to influenza viruses
mix_items.summary: Influenza viruses constantly shapeshift to evade recognition by the immune system. This shapeshifting occurs in critical proteins like hemagglutinin (HA), which controls how the virus attaches to human cells before entering them. Influenza viruses can evade immunity in two major ways: through the gradual accumulation of mutations that make HA harder for the immune system to recognize or through reassortment events that can introduce substantially different viral proteins and potentially lead to flu pandemics. To address this challenge, seasonal flu vaccines remain the primary approach because they can be developed to target the flu viruses circulating most predominantly in a given season.

mix_items.title: Algorithm improves detection of differentially expressed genes in large single-cell trajectory data sets
mix_items.summary: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is a method for measuring gene expression in individual cells, allowing observation of various cellular processes, including cell differentiation, the cell cycle and stimulus response, for each unique cell instead of averaging across millions of cells. It provides high-resolution snapshots of biological processes. However, it does not track the same cell continuously over time. To address this limitation, trajectory inference approaches have been developed that computationally arrange cellular snapshots along an inferred developmental trajectory known as pseudotime.

mix_items.title: Firelight may have sparked human storytelling by extending social hours
mix_items.summary: New research from the University of St Andrews has developed a novel hypothesis of how firelight was critical to the evolution of sophisticated storytelling.

mix_items.title: Muddying the waters makes stickleback fish more coordinated, study finds
mix_items.summary: Stickleback fish can change their social behavior to help them find food in cloudy water, according to a new University of Bristol study published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

mix_items.title: Survey reveals marine biodiversity hotspot needs protection
mix_items.summary: An environmental DNA study by a multi-institutional research collaboration has revealed distinct regions of extraordinary marine biodiversity that can help inform management of a proposed marine park in Western Australia's Exmouth Gulf.

mix_items.title: Training the mind and emotional skills may support brain health after 65
mix_items.summary: Education, intellectually stimulating work and an active lifestyle help preserve cognitive abilities in adults over 65 and lead to more effective verbal expression and stronger cognitive performance. But there is another important factor: emotions. The way we recognize and interpret them can significantly influence the efficiency of cognitive processes as we age.

mix_items.title: LEDs let archaeologists see the past in a new light
mix_items.summary: An archaeological excavation is a little like eating a layered cake: Once you have removed a layer, you cannot put it back. The problem becomes even trickier if two layers look almost exactly the same. Researchers from Aarhus University and Moesgaard Museum in Denmark have now developed a relatively inexpensive multispectral imaging system that gives archaeologists more ways of looking at the soil before they dig into it.

mix_items.title: Ghanaian adults' diets fall short on sustainability, survey finds
mix_items.summary: There has been a rapid increase in cardiovascular and metabolic conditions in sub-Saharan Africa. What is the link between sustainable diets that are nutritious, environmentally friendly, economically affordable and socioculturally acceptable, and cardiometabolic conditions? An international research team led by Prof. Dr. Ina Danquah, Hertz Chair for Innovation for Planetary Health in the Transdisciplinary Research Area "Sustainable Futures" and director at the Center for Development Research (ZEF) at the University of Bonn, investigated this question among Ghanaian adults living in various locations for an article published in The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition.

mix_items.title: To promote climate action, emotion may matter more than information
mix_items.summary: Every year, public authorities and nongovernmental organizations spend millions on communication campaigns designed to encourage people to take action on climate change. But which strategies work best? Should campaigns rely on fear or positive messages, prioritize facts or appeal to emotions, and focus on words or visuals?

mix_items.title: Study highlights risk groups for a severe side effect of diabetes treatment
mix_items.summary: Patients with type 2 diabetes who have high blood glucose levels, low body weight or a history of ketoacidosis are at increased risk of developing this serious condition when treated with so-called SGLT2 inhibitors. A study led by researchers at Karolinska Institutet also shows that the risk persists throughout the entire course of treatment.

mix_items.title: Giant impact could have formed an intact moon within five hours, simulations suggest
mix_items.summary: New Southwest Research Institute (SwRI) modeling, conducted in collaboration with scientists at the University of Arizona, shows fundamental differences in how the moon may have formed from the giant impact that created the Earth–moon system. The new results used state-of-the-art computational techniques that factor in the material strength of the two colliding planets. These impact simulations could change how researchers understand moon formation and may help constrain the timing of the event. The research is published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

mix_items.title: Elementary school teachers report increased student hunger and anxiety after universal free school meals ended
mix_items.summary: A recent study published in the Journal of Nutrition Education and Behavior explored elementary school teachers' experiences before and after the end of the federal universal free school meals (UFSM) policy. Researchers found that teachers perceived the policy had helped reduce student hunger and family stress, while its expiration was associated with increased hunger, anxiety about meal costs and decreased participation in school meal programs.

mix_items.title: Cancer cachexia: How a tumor protein drives wasting in the body
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Helmholtz Munich, the Heidelberg Faculty of Medicine at Heidelberg University, the German Center for Diabetes Research (DZD) and the Technical University of Munich (TUM) have identified a previously unknown mechanism that can drive cancer cachexia—a wasting process in the body that primarily affects muscle and fat tissue.

mix_items.title: Salt of the Earth: How Egypt's coastal sabkhas tell a story of climate and change
mix_items.summary: Have you ever walked across a salt flat so expansive it feels like another planet? That's what it's like standing in Egypt's coastal sabkhas—those otherworldly landscapes where the ground crunches beneath your feet and the air shimmers with heat. These aren't just barren wastelands; they're living laboratories that record the pulse of our changing climate.

mix_items.title: First touch, faster play: Study reveals the body and ball movements associated with quicker soccer passing
mix_items.summary: In soccer, the quality of the first touch is integral to shaping a player's subsequent actions. Despite its importance, there is limited scientific evidence regarding which specific movement characteristics are associated with effective first-touch performance.

mix_items.title: How does the cancer drug Keytruda work? And how is it different from chemo?
mix_items.summary: From today, the Australian government will expand Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) access to the drug Keytruda for three additional types of cancer.

mix_items.title: Your smartwatch may be lying to you about how many calories you burned
mix_items.summary: If you're depending on your smartwatch to tell you the truth about how many calories you burned during a workout—well, don't.

mix_items.title: Canada's Labrador Shelf preserves climate records once thought erased by ice
mix_items.summary: The Labrador Shelf is a shallow marine area on the margin of the Labrador Sea in the North Atlantic off the east coast of Canada. During the last ice age, this region was covered by the Laurentide Ice Sheet, one of the largest ice masses in Earth's history, which once covered vast parts of North America.

mix_items.title: A roadmap for animal-free chemical testing
mix_items.summary: For many years, the European Union has pursued a policy aimed at the replacement, reduction and refinement of animal testing (the 3Rs principle). To put the ethical principle of the 3Rs into practice, the European Commission has published a roadmap for the gradual phaseout of animal testing in the safety assessment of chemicals.

mix_items.title: Peppermint oil lowers blood pressure in just 20 days
mix_items.summary: Peppermint oil may have an unexpected benefit for people with mildly high blood pressure. Adults who took a small dose twice daily for 20 days saw their systolic blood pressure fall by an average of 8.5 mmHg, while a placebo group showed little change. Researchers say the inexpensive oil could eventually provide a simple additional option for managing elevated blood pressure.

mix_items.title: Exercise may work better for keeping weight off than losing it
mix_items.summary: Exercise may not be a powerful weight-loss tool on its own, but it appears to play a much bigger role in preventing lost weight from returning. By preserving muscle, supporting metabolism, improving fat burning, and regulating appetite and blood sugar, regular activity can make long-term weight maintenance easier.

mix_items.title: Multilingual people may have brains up to 13 years younger
mix_items.summary: People who speak several languages may have brains that age more slowly, with four-language speakers showing brains that appeared about 13 years younger than those of monolinguals. Starting earlier and becoming highly fluent were also linked to a stronger effect.

mix_items.title: This yeast supplement may boost cancer-fighting immunity
mix_items.summary: A simple yeast-based food supplement may help restore the immune system’s ability to fight cancer, according to new research in mice. Scientists found that yeast beta-glucan reprogrammed early immune cells in the bone marrow, leading to stronger, longer-lasting cancer-fighting responses against colorectal, skin, and breast cancer cells.

mix_items.title: Tooth count may predict survival after pancreatic cancer surgery
mix_items.summary: Pancreatic cancer patients with at least 21 natural teeth survived nearly two years longer after surgery than those with fewer teeth in a study of 339 people. Researchers suspect tooth loss may reflect decades of inflammation, frailty, nutrition, and other factors tied to the body’s overall resilience.

mix_items.title: This gut microbe may help keep you strong as you age
mix_items.summary: Scientists have linked a specific gut bacterium, Roseburia inulinivorans, to stronger muscles in both humans and mice. Older adults who carried it had 29% greater handgrip strength, while treated mice gained about 30% more grip strength and developed larger, more fast-twitch muscle fibers. The bacterium was also less common in older people. Researchers say it could eventually become a probiotic candidate for helping combat age-related muscle loss.

mix_items.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals ancient waterproofing secrets
mix_items.summary: Scientists analyzing a 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck found that its hull was coated with pine tar and, in one area, a mixture of tar and beeswax. Pollen trapped in those ancient coatings acted like a geographic fingerprint, revealing the landscapes surrounding the ship when repairs were made.

mix_items.title: A lost mega-cliff may explain the Grand Canyon’s missing billion years
mix_items.summary: A colossal cliff system created as the supercontinent Rodinia broke apart may have exposed the heart of the Grand Canyon nearly a billion years before the Colorado River carved it. The ancient landscape could also help explain why enormous sections of North America’s geological record appear to be missing.

mix_items.title: “One-in-a-million” sea creature fossil preserves soft tissue for 450 million years
mix_items.summary: Scientists have identified exceptionally rare soft tissue preserved in a 450-million-year-old crinoid fossil, more than 200 million years older than the first dinosaurs. Its delicate tube feet offer a remarkable new window into how some of Earth’s earliest reef animals lived, fed, and evolved.

mix_items.title: A new Ice Age species was hiding in la brea tar pits fossils for decades
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered a new extinct amphibian species hiding in the fossil collections of Los Angeles’ La Brea Tar Pits. Named Spea labreae, the Ice Age spadefoot toad is an exceptionally rare find—only one other extinct Pleistocene amphibian has ever been identified in North America. Its bones had been sitting in collections since the 1950s before a researcher noticed features that set it apart from known species.
